pr_title: Presence of bearer token should cancel exec action
pr_body:
**What type of PR is this?**
/kind bug

**What this PR does / why we need it**:
If a bearer token is present in a request/config, the exec credential plugin should accept that as the chosen method of authentication. Judging by an [earlier comment in exec.go](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/c18bc7e9f7a27d7d197053d98c52896e1dc3bb3e/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/plugin/pkg/client/auth/exec/exec.go#L217), this was already the intention. This would however not work since `UpdateTransportConfig` would set the `GetCert` callback which would then get called by the transport, triggering the exec plugin action even with a token present in the request. See linked issue for further details.

**Which issue(s) this PR fixes**:
Fixes #87369

**Special notes for your reviewer**:

**Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?**:
<!--
If no, just write "NONE" in the release-note block below.

For more information on release notes see: https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/release-notes.md
-->
```release-note
Fixed ambiguous behavior when bearer token (kubectl --token=..) and an exec credential plugin was configured in the same context - the bearer token now takes precedence.
```

> LGTM, but I would like to see a `kubectl get --token $TOKEN pods` style test to prove that this actually overrides the `exec` plugin in the way that we expect it to.

I had never written that type of test in this code base before so it took some time to get something working. First iteration of such test did _not_ trigger the exec credential plugin action so I struggled for quite some time trying to figure out what would cause the behavior to be different with the running test server vs. my own servers (including kind) where it was easy to trigger. Turns out the GetCert callback is only called if the server advertised client certificate authentication capabilities in the TLS handshake! So with that added to the test server configuration the exec action is indeed triggered even with `--token=xxx` provided in the request. 

You can verify by running the integration test (`make test-cmd WHAT="exec_credentials"`) with and without the early return in the `UpdateTransportConfig` function - the kubectl call is done with `--token=admin-token` and should thus not trigger the exec action.

Since I hadn't written this type of test before I probably did a couple of rookie mistakes - I tried looking at other tests of the same type for inspiration, but any feedback is appreciated :)

issue_context.title: kubecetl client-go exec credentials plugin should use new valid token as soon as stored rather than old expired
issue_context.body:
<!-- Please use this template while reporting a bug and provide as much info as possible. Not doing so may result in your bug not being addressed in a timely manner. Thanks!

If the matter is security related, please disclose it privately via https://kubernetes.io/security/
-->

**What happened**:

With the exec credentials plugin configured in my kubeconf, *and* a stale/expired token present in the same file issuing e.g. `kubectl get pod` triggers the authentication flow as handled by the plugin - once the flow is returned to kubectl (by printing the ExecCredential object) the new token is stored to the kubeconfig *but* not immediately used to resolve the `kubectl get pod` request, leading to:

`error: You must be logged in to the server (Unauthorized)`

Immediately issuing `kubectl get pod` again works as kubectl now seem to use the credentials (token) stored following the first request.

**What you expected to happen**:

That kubectl would read the new token as fetched by the exec credential plugin and use it already for the first command issued. 

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

1. Configure the kubernetes API server with the OIDC authenticator enabled.
2. Configure kubectl to use an exec credential plugin printing the token received out of band.
3. Verify that the token was indeed written to the kubeconf file.
4. See that the first kubectl command failed.
5. See that the next identical command succeeds.

**Anything else we need to know?**:

This works as expected when there is *no* token previously stored in the kubeconf - the behavior is only triggered when there is a token stored but it expired, or for whatever other reason not accepted by the API server.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`): 1.14, also tried with 1.17
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration:
- OS (e.g: `cat /etc/os-release`): Mac OS for kubectl client
- Kernel (e.g. `uname -a`):
- Install tools:
- Network plugin and version (if this is a network-related bug):
- Others:
comments:
Thanks for looking into it @enj . You are indeed correct in your assumption that I'm using a [custom exec plugin](https://github.com/Bisnode/kubectl-login) which stores the token in the `KUBECONFIG` after retrieval. I'd love to learn why this should not be done, but the problem remains also without persisting the token after retrieval. Basically the steps to reproduce could be reduced to these:

1. A `KUBECONFIG` containing an expired token.
2. The same `KUBECONFIG` configuring an exec plugin which retrieves a valid token out of band and echoes it.

Expected behavior: The valid token retrieved is used for the subsequent authentication.
Possibly expected behavior: The exec plugin flow not started (or exited with a warning) due to an expired token being present in the `KUBECONFIG`.

Current behavior seems to acknowledge the invalid token and hence tries to retrieve a new, valid one - which it then discards as soon as it arrives.

Seems we can reduce it even further by removing the token altogether from the `KUBECONFIG` file and instead provide it directly. So the only step needed to reproduce is essentially this:

1. A `KUBECONFIG` configuring an exec plugin which retrieves a valid token out of band and echoes it as part of an [ExecCredential object](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authentication/#input-and-output-formats).

Now any `kubectl --token=<expired_token> <command>` will trigger the exec plugin to retrieve a valid token, but will still not use it for subsequent authentication.

> Now any `kubectl --token=<expired_token> <command>` will trigger the exec plugin to retrieve a valid token, but will still not use it for subsequent authentication.

This one is caused by config merging with clientcmd overrides:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f13c5c3d1cdbb983c3e3d7a1b2a1ef803d24fcb/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/clientcmd/client_config.go#L425-L434

and exec.Auth not being added in this switch:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0f13c5c3d1cdbb983c3e3d7a1b2a1ef803d24fcb/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/transport/round_trippers.go#L44
Interesting, thanks @mikedanese. Will add it to the switch along with some tests and if everything works out well I'll submit a PR next week.

Having spent some time on this in the debugger, it seems somewhat more intricate than I first thought. Turns out the exec plugin is executed whether the `--token` presented is invalid _or valid_ - the exec action is actually called before the first call is even dispatched. This due to the exec credential plugin possibly being needed to setup the client certificate requested for the transport. Once the exec plugin's `UpdateTransportConfig` is called it assign the authenticators `cert` function to `c.TLS.GetCert`:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fb6f5d739b08e049b188806d6e33099f85fad2fe/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/plugin/pkg/client/auth/exec/exec.go#L188

..which is then called when setting up the transport, thus triggering the exec plugin regardless of a token being present or not:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fb6f5d739b08e049b188806d6e33099f85fad2fe/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/transport/transport.go#L94-L102

Since the exec plugin has no way of knowing whether a token or a client certificate will be returned by the exec action, this kind of makes sense. It however defeats letting any `--token` present to override the exec plugin, which clearly seems to be the intent:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/fb6f5d739b08e049b188806d6e33099f85fad2fe/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/plugin/pkg/client/auth/exec/exec.go#L216-L221

Possible options here that I can think of:
1. Keep (and fix) behavior of letting `--token` override the exec plugin. This looks doable by adding a check for token auth early in the exec.go's `UpdateTransportConfig` method body:
```
if c.HasTokenAuth() {
    return nil
}
```
But might be there are consequences to this I'm not aware of.

2. Remove the behavior of letting `--token` override the exec plugin being called.

3. A third, more complex option, would be to keep the token override but dispatch to the exec credential plugin should the response from the first call with the token come back with a 401. This was what I originally believed was the intent as my first tests always included an invalid token. While this behavior seems nice I'm more and more thinking it may violate the principle of least surprise. Either you present a token and use that for auth or you let the exec plugin fetch the credentials for you.

What do you guys think?

As a colleague just made me aware of, certain tools like kubetail seem to have kubectl call the exec plugin so many times that eventually the `onRotateListWarningLength` threshold of 1000 is reached and warn logs (exec:201) start spewing - even though no certificate (and hence no rotation) should be involved. This has me more convinced that the first option is the right one, skipping the client TLS ceremonies should a token be present for authentication.

review_comments: Please add a comment explaining in detail (i.e. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/87369#issuecomment-585579312) why we basically need the same check twice.
if we already have a client cert/key, should that take precedence as well and prevent calling the exec plugin?

I think that makes sense, yes. This PR addressed a real problem we experienced with our exec plugin using tokens, and the client certificate scenario wasn't something I considered - I don't even know what the current behavior there is to be honest, but I could certainly look into supporting that case as well if you want. With that said, I think the single argument of `--token` makes it a _lot_ more likely to be used ad-hoc than client certificates, which requires something like three(?) file locations to be provided.
I think the current state of the PR is coherent w.r.t. token auth. A follow up issue to discuss/resolve treatment of client cert auth is fine with me

Thinking on this a bit more, maybe this should be the first line in this function.  As it stands, it attempts to configure token auth via the `c.Wrap` call but then skips the cert auth.

It may make more sense for `UpdateTransportConfig` to do nothing when `c.HasTokenAuth()` returns `true` instead of doing "half" of what it is supposed to do.  We still want the `req.Header.Get("Authorization") != ""` logic below because round trippers can be arbitrarily stacked via `c.Wrap`.
Agreed - moved to top of function.
